::: {.lead}
Today is presentation day. In lecture 28 you planned your course project,
built the data sheet and wrote the first draft of the report. Now you turn
the report into **five slides**, **check** every slide, and **present**
your project to the class in **three minutes**. Sami, a student at
*Sunrise Company*, presents the canteen sales; you present your own topic.
After each talk, the class gives short **feedback**, which you use for the
final version in lecture 30. Every section ends with a lab task.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary presentation-outline slides-from-outline speaker-notes presenter-view ai-image check-ai-output ai-use-statement rehearsal peer-feedback >}}

## 29.1 From the report to five slides

A three-minute talk needs only **five slides** (@fig-five).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 29.1 — Five slides"}
1. **Title:** the topic and your name.
2. **Question:** your project question in one sentence.
3. **Chart:** the answer in a picture, with a title.
4. **Insights:** two short, checked sentences with numbers.
5. **End:** thanks, questions, and your AI-use line.

Make them quickly from the report: give the five titles **Heading 1** and
use **Slides from Outline** (lecture 27), or ask an AI tool for an outline
of five slides from your report. Then paste the chart **as a link**, choose
a theme or Designer (lecture 17), and write few words on each slide.
:::

![Five slides for a three-minute talk.](images/five-slides.png){#fig-five width=100%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 29.1 — Sami's slides"}
1. Sami's report has the headings of lecture 28. Sami makes five Heading 1
   lines and runs Slides from Outline.
2. On slide 3, Sami pastes the column chart of the total by item as a link.
3. Slide 4 gets two insights: "Sandwiches earned the most: 138 JD." and
   "Tea sold the most cups: 150."
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Copying whole paragraphs of the report onto the slides. The class reads
instead of listening. Put a few words on the slide and say the rest.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Lab task · Your five slides"}
1. Make `talk.pptx` with five slides from your report (Slides from Outline
   or an AI outline).
2. Paste your chart as a link, and write two insights on slide 4.

*Your result:* `talk.pptx` with five slides.
:::

## 29.2 Check every slide

AI makes slides fast, and it can also make mistakes. Check every slide
before you present (@fig-checks).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 29.2 — Four checks"}
- **Accuracy:** every number on a slide is the same as in your Excel
  sheet.
- **Claims:** every sentence is shown by your data. "Sandwiches earned the
  most" is shown; "everyone loves sandwiches" is not.
- **Pictures:** an AI picture fits the topic, shows no wrong text, and has
  no unfair picture of a group of people (lecture 21).
- **Honesty:** the last slide says where AI helped (lecture 23).
:::

![Four checks for every slide.](images/slide-checks.png){#fig-checks width=100%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 29.2 — Two mistakes on Sami's slides"}
1. Slide 3 says "Total: 451 JD". Excel says 415 JD: two digits were
   swapped. Sami updates the link and corrects the text.
2. The AI wrote "Everyone loves sandwiches." Sami changes it to
   "Sandwiches earned the most: 138 JD."
:::

{{< sim file="sims/deck-checker.html" poster="sims/deck-checker.png" title="Deck Checker: ready to present?" height="880" >}}

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Checking only the chart and not the text around it. A wrong number in a
sentence is as bad as a wrong bar.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Lab task · Check your slides"}
1. In **Deck Checker**, mark Sami's five slides.
2. Check your own slides with the four checks, and fix every problem.

*Your result:* five checked slides.
:::

## 29.3 Present in three minutes

A good talk is planned and practised (@fig-presenter).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 29.3 — Presenting"}
- Write short **speaker notes** under each slide: reminders, not a text
  to read.
- Start the slide show with **Presenter View**: you see the slide, the
  next slide, your notes and a timer (lecture 18). The class sees only the
  slide.
- About **30–40 seconds per slide**. Do one **rehearsal** with a timer
  before your turn.
- Look at the class, speak slowly, and end with your main insight.
- Answer questions honestly. If you do not know, say so and say how you
  could find out.
:::

![Presenter View.](images/presenter-view.png){#fig-presenter width=100%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 29.3 — Sami's three minutes"}
1. Sami's notes on slide 3: "Sandwiches earned the most: 138 JD. Tea sold
   the most cups."
2. In the rehearsal, the talk takes 4 minutes. Sami cuts one sentence on
   each slide: now it takes 3 minutes.
3. A classmate asks: "Why did tea sell more cups?" Sami says: "My data
   does not show why. A short survey could tell us."
:::

{{< sim file="../week-09/sims/talk-planner.html" poster="../week-09/sims/talk-planner.png" title="Talk Planner: a five-slide talk" height="900" >}}

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Reading the slides aloud with your back to the class. Use the notes in
Presenter View, and look at the people.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Lab task · Rehearse and present"}
1. In **Talk Planner**, plan a five-slide talk of about three minutes.
2. Write speaker notes, do one rehearsal with a timer, and present your
   project to the class.

*Your result:* speaker notes and a three-minute talk.
:::

## 29.4 Give and use peer feedback

After each talk, the class gives **peer feedback** in three short lines
(@fig-feedback).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 29.4 — Peer feedback"}
- **One thing that works:** name it exactly.
- **One question:** something you want to know.
- **One idea:** one change that would make the project better.

Feedback is about the work, not the person. Write down the feedback you
receive, and choose what to change for the final version.
:::

![Peer feedback in three lines.](images/feedback-card.png){#fig-feedback width=100%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 29.4 — Feedback for Sami"}
1. Works: "The chart is clear and has a title."
2. Question: "Why did tea sell more cups?"
3. Idea: "Show the week totals too." Sami adds a small table of the week
   totals to the report for lecture 30.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Writing "Nice!" or "Bad." as feedback. Nobody can act on it. Say what
works, ask one real question, and give one idea.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Lab task · Feedback"}
1. Write three-line feedback on two other talks.
2. Write down the feedback you received, and choose one change for the
   final version.

*Your result:* two feedback cards and one planned change.
:::

## Case study: Presentation Day

During the presentations, six things happen: a linked chart shows old
numbers, a slide has a claim that the data does not show, time runs out,
a classmate asks a hard question, a student reads every word, and the
class gives feedback. The Game challenge of the interactive lesson uses
these situations. In the mini-game below you choose the best thing to do
each time.

{{< sim file="sims/presentation-day.html" poster="sims/presentation-day.png" title="Presentation Day: six situations" kind="game" height="460" >}}

Upload `talk.pptx` (with speaker notes) and your feedback notes to the
e-learning platform.

*Your result:* two files.
:::

## Exercises

1. Name the five slides of a three-minute talk.
2. How can you make the slides quickly from your report?
3. How long should each slide take in a three-minute talk?
4. Name the four checks for every slide.
5. Excel says 415 JD; a slide says 451 JD. Which check fails?
6. Why is "Everyone loves sandwiches" a problem?
7. What do you see in Presenter View that the class does not see?
8. What is a rehearsal?
9. What do you say when you do not know the answer to a question?
10. Name the three lines of peer feedback.

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. Title, question, chart, insights, end.
2. Heading 1 lines and Slides from Outline, or an AI outline from the
   report.
3. About 30–40 seconds.
4. Accuracy, claims, pictures, honesty.
5. Accuracy.
6. The data shows sales, not what everyone loves.
7. The next slide, the notes and a timer.
8. Saying the whole talk once with a timer before the real talk.
9. Say that you do not know, and how you could find out.
10. One thing that works, one question, one idea.
:::
